With four piles, though, the mover always has a choice among the non-blocked piles, so the strategy space is much richer and I'll need to think about it in terms of overall tempo — how the total move count across piles determines who runs out of options first.

The game continues as long as at least two piles remain nonempty, since with two or more nonempty piles the mover always has an unblocked option; the trouble only arises once a single pile is left. If that last pile is unblocked, the mover empties it and the opponent is stuck with no moves and loses—so the critical question becomes who is forced to move right when only one pile remains.

This means emptying the second-to-last pile is bad, since it leaves the opponent with a free pile to win from. With two nonempty piles where one is blocked, the mover wins if the free pile exceeds the blocked one; if instead the blocked designation comes from a pile that's actually empty, the mover wins whenever the two piles are unequal.
